scenarios.name: nginx worker starts a shell
scenarios.note: depth-1 ancestry from a network-facing service

scenarios.name: php-fpm worker descendant starts bash
scenarios.note: depth-2 ancestry: service > helper > shell

scenarios.name: php-fpm runs an allowlisted image converter via sh
scenarios.note: suppressed by an allowlist entry with an owner and an expiry

scenarios.name: gunicorn app shells out to git
scenarios.note: RESIDUAL FALSE POSITIVE: legitimate, not allowlisted; needs an owner decision

scenarios.name: admin reloads nginx from an ssh session
scenarios.note: parent is the admin shell, not the service

scenarios.name: PID reuse: a benign shell reuses pid 61000 of a former nginx child
scenarios.note: identity (pid + start time) prevents misattribution; a pid-only join would alert

scenarios.name: shell writes /etc/cron.d
scenarios.note: non-package-manager writer creates a system cron entry

scenarios.name: dpkg updates /etc/cron.d during an upgrade
scenarios.note: package manager writer

scenarios.name: configuration management writes /etc/cron.d
scenarios.note: suppressed by an allowlist entry with an owner and an expiry

scenarios.name: admin edits /etc/cron.d/backup with vim
scenarios.note: RESIDUAL FALSE POSITIVE: a legitimate manual change; correlate with a change record

scenarios.name: user crontab written by the crontab binary
scenarios.note: KNOWN MISS: the per-user spool is excluded because crontab(1) is its legitimate writer

scenarios.name: shell installs a unit whose ExecStart is under /tmp
scenarios.note: persistence via a unit pointing at a world-writable path

scenarios.name: dpkg installs a service unit
scenarios.note: package manager writer, ExecStart in /usr

scenarios.name: admin installs an app unit under /opt
scenarios.note: non-package writer but ExecStart is not under a writable directory

scenarios.name: developer user unit under /home
scenarios.note: RESIDUAL FALSE POSITIVE: user units under /home are a normal developer workflow

scenarios.name: binary in /tmp connects to a public address
scenarios.note: exe under a world-writable directory with a public destination

scenarios.name: binary in /dev/shm connects out over 443
scenarios.note: same rule, TLS port: the port is not the signal

scenarios.name: admin curls a public HTTPS endpoint
scenarios.note: ordinary exe path

scenarios.name: CI toolchain unpacked in /tmp fetches dependencies
scenarios.note: RESIDUAL FALSE POSITIVE: build tools run from /tmp; allowlist by exe hash or run builds elsewhere

scenarios.name: system bash makes an outbound connection
scenarios.note: KNOWN MISS: the exe path is ordinary, so path-based egress logic does not see it

scenarios.name: python reads /etc/shadow as www-data
scenarios.note: unexpected reader of the shadow file

scenarios.name: binary in /tmp reads cloud credentials
scenarios.note: credential file read by an unexpected process

scenarios.name: unix_chkpwd reads /etc/shadow at login
scenarios.note: the designed reader; also covered in the background noise

scenarios.name: backup agent reads shadow and ssh keys
scenarios.note: suppressed by an allowlist entry with an owner and an expiry

scenarios.name: nightly audit scanner reads /etc/shadow

scenarios.name: shell drops a NOPASSWD sudoers file as www-data

scenarios.name: write to /etc/ld.so.preload

scenarios.name: visudo edits /etc/sudoers
scenarios.note: designed editor

scenarios.name: useradd updates passwd, shadow and group
scenarios.note: designed account tool

scenarios.name: admin applies an approved sudoers.d change with tee

scenarios.name: execution from an anonymous memory file
scenarios.note: fileless execution pattern

scenarios.name: execution of a binary that was deleted after launch
scenarios.note: the file was unlinked to hide it

scenarios.name: ordinary exec of a system binary
scenarios.note: nothing unusual about the path

scenarios.name: logrotate rotates auth.log

scenarios.name: admin truncates a huge log to free disk

scenarios.name: the same suspicious write repeated 50 times

scenarios.name: a detectable write that reaches the pipeline 125 seconds late
scenarios.note: event time and ingest time diverge: detection latency is dominated by ingestion, not by the rule
